```{python}
#| include: false
import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
from great_tables import GT

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
df = pd.read_csv("data/actn3_yang2003.csv")
genotypes = ["RR", "RX", "XX"]
tab = df.set_index("group").loc[["Sprint", "Control"]][genotypes].to_numpy()
```

# Question

**Is there a "sprinting gene"?** The *α-actinin-3* gene (**ACTN3**) encodes a protein
expressed in fast-twitch muscle fibers. The **R577X** polymorphism creates a premature
stop codon: the **XX** genotype produces no functioning actinin-3 at all.

Data: @yang2003 — genotype distributions for elite sprint athletes (n=107), endurance
athletes (n=194), and controls (n=436). This is the same case study used in
*Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data* (Lock⁵).

## Data

```{python}
#| echo: false
GT(df).fmt_number(columns=["n", "RR", "RX", "XX"], decimals=0) \
    .tab_header(title="ACTN3 R577X genotype counts (Yang et al. 2003)")
```

# Exploratory analysis

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "ACTN3 genotype distribution by group (proportions)"
long = df.melt(id_vars=["group", "n"], value_vars=genotypes,
               var_name="Genotype", value_name="count")
long["prop"] = long["count"] / long["n"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
sns.barplot(data=long, x="Genotype", y="prop", hue="group", ax=ax)
ax.set_ylabel("Proportion of group")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Elite sprinters show a markedly **lower proportion of the XX genotype** (5.6% vs
18.3% in controls) and a **higher R-allele frequency** (72.0% vs 55.7%).

# Hypothesis tests

**H₀:** ACTN3 genotype distribution is the same for sprinters and controls
**Hₐ:** distributions differ

```{python}
#| echo: false
chi2, p_chi, dof, exp = stats.chi2_contingency(tab)
print(f"Chi-square test of homogeneity: χ² = {chi2:.2f}, df = {dof}, p = {p_chi:.6f}")
```

## Randomization test (Lock5 approach)

We simulate 100,000 shuffles of group labels under H₀ and recompute χ² each time:

```{python}
#| echo: false
counts_geno = tab.sum(axis=0)
geno_vec = np.concatenate([np.repeat("RR", counts_geno[0]),
                           np.repeat("RX", counts_geno[1]),
                           np.repeat("XX", counts_geno[2])])
lab_vec = np.array(["Sprint"] * tab[0].sum() + ["Control"] * tab[1].sum())
nperm = 100_000
perm_stats = np.empty(nperm)
for i in range(nperm):
    g = geno_vec[rng.permutation(len(geno_vec))]
    ct = np.array([[np.sum(g[lab_vec == "Sprint"] == geno) for geno in genotypes],
                   [np.sum(g[lab_vec == "Control"] == geno) for geno in genotypes]])
    perm_stats[i] = stats.chi2_contingency(ct)[0]
p_perm = np.mean(perm_stats >= chi2)
print(f"Permutation test p-value = {p_perm:.5f}")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Randomization distribution of χ² under H₀"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.hist(perm_stats, bins=60, color="#7b9fc7", edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(chi2, color="crimson", lw=2,
           label=f"observed χ² = {chi2:.2f}")
ax.set_xlabel("χ² statistic"); ax.set_ylabel("Frequency"); ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Two-proportion test: XX genotype

```{python}
#| echo: false
xx_s, n_s = tab[0, 2], tab[0].sum()
xx_c, n_c = tab[1, 2], tab[1].sum()
pooled = (xx_s + xx_c) / (n_s + n_c)
se = np.sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * (1 / n_s + 1 / n_c))
z = (xx_s / n_s - xx_c / n_c) / se
p_z = 2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(z))
print(f"Sprinters XX: {xx_s}/{n_s} = {xx_s/n_s:.3f} vs Controls: {xx_c}/{n_c} = {xx_c/n_c:.3f}")
print(f"z = {z:.3f}, p-value = {p_z:.5f}")
```

# Interval estimate: R-allele advantage

Bootstrap 95% CI for the difference in R-allele frequency (sprint − control):

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Bootstrap distribution of difference in R-allele frequency"
sprint_alleles = np.array([1] * (2*tab[0,0] + tab[0,1]) + [0] * (2*tab[0,2] + tab[0,1]))
ctrl_alleles  = np.array([1] * (2*tab[1,0] + tab[1,1]) + [0] * (2*tab[1,2] + tab[1,1]))
boot = np.array([sprint_alleles[rng.integers(0, len(sprint_alleles), len(sprint_alleles))].mean()
                 - ctrl_alleles[rng.integers(0, len(ctrl_alleles), len(ctrl_alleles))].mean()
                 for _ in range(nperm)])
ci = np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5])
print(f"95% CI: ({ci[0]:.3f}, {ci[1]:.3f})")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.hist(boot, bins=60, color="#8fbf8f", edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(ci[0], color="crimson", ls="--"); ax.axvline(ci[1], color="crimson", ls="--")
ax.set_xlabel("p_R(sprint) − p_R(control)"); ax.set_ylabel("Frequency")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# Decision

| Method | Result | p-value / CI |
|---|---|---|
| χ² homogeneity (Sprint vs Control) | χ² = 19.54, df = 2 | p < 0.0001 |
| Randomization test (100k shuffles) | — | p < 0.0001 |
| Two-proportion z (XX genotype) | z = −3.24 | p = 0.0012 |
| Bootstrap 95% CI (R-allele diff) | — | (0.093, 0.231) |

**Conclusion:** All three methods agree — reject H₀. Genotype distribution differs
significantly between elite sprinters and controls. The XX (no-actinin-3) genotype is
**under-represented** among elite sprinters (5.6% vs 18.3%), and sprinters carry the
R allele at a rate ~16 percentage points higher than controls.

**Statistical answer: yes — there is strong evidence for a "sprinting gene" association.**
Caveats: observational data (association ≠ causation), modest sprinter sample size
(only 6 XX sprinters), and elite athletic performance involves many genes and
environmental factors.
